name: Model Risk and Bias Testing
title: Model Risk and Bias Testing
answer: Model risk and bias testing covers the chance that a model produces wrong, misleading or unfair outputs and the controls used to find and limit that harm. In finance it touches credit scoring, fraud detection, anti money laundering, underwriting, pricing, trading and customer service. Bias testing looks at whether outcomes differ systematically across groups defined by law or policy, and whether those differences come from data, features, labels or proxies. The scope also includes model inventory, tiering, documentation, validation and ongoing monitoring across the model lifecycle.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Work runs on data pipelines, feature stores, model registries, version control and validation environments that keep training and test data separate from production. Teams use SQL, Python, notebooks, workflow schedulers and monitoring dashboards, with logs and metadata captured for every run. Compute may be on premises, in a private cloud or in a public cloud, and access controls, encryption and audit trails apply to data and model artifacts. A test harness needs to reproduce a model version, replay data, run bias and performance checks, and store results for review.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start with a model inventory and tier models by materiality, then run independent validation before deployment and at set intervals after. Data quality checks look for missing values, drift, leakage and unrepresentative samples, while bias tests compare outcomes across groups using metrics such as selection rate, disparate impact ratio, equal opportunity difference and calibration. Backtesting, challenger models, stress tests and sensitivity analysis show how results change when inputs or assumptions shift. Findings are documented with evidence, rated by severity, assigned to owners and tracked to remediation or revalidation. Human review and sign off sit above the automated checks for high tier models.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk work sits inside model risk management, fair lending, privacy and data protection rules, with supervisory expectations for documentation, challenge, audit and accountability. Provenance means knowing where training data came from, what rights attach to it, how it was transformed and which model version produced a given output. Individuals may have rights to explanation, correction or contest, and firms need records that support adverse action notices and regulatory inquiries. Third party models and data add vendor risk, so contracts, model cards, lineage records and audit rights matter. The site's compliance and regulation section, currently 215 pages, shows how many overlapping expectations apply.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Testing is moving from periodic review toward continuous monitoring, with automated checks for drift, bias and performance running alongside production traffic. Generative AI and large language models bring new tests for hallucination, prompt sensitivity, data leakage and group level harm, where the same prompt can produce different answers. Regulators and auditors are asking for more evidence, clearer model cards and stronger human oversight, and the site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits as one sign of that pressure. Expect more convergence between model risk, data security and third party risk, and more use of synthetic data and causal methods to test fairness. The direction is toward traceable, repeatable testing that a non specialist can review.
